input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Define the evaluation workflow: how sections are sampled or aggregated, human reviewer procedures for reviewer-style scores, and automated audits. Precisely define metrics: citation coverage, hallucination rate (unsupported assertions per section), and reviewer scoring rubric. Explain how citation coverage and unsupported assertions are measured (e.g., presence/absence of explicit source citations tied to assertions), any inter-annotator agreement checks, and the statistical comparisons or tests used to compare systems.

output:
\textbf{Evaluation overview.}
We evaluate generated sections with a mixed protocol combining manual reviewer judgments and automated audits. The protocol is organized to (i) measure explicit citation usage relative to asserted facts, (ii) quantify unsupported or hallucinated assertions, and (iii) collect reviewer-style quality scores that reflect factuality, citation adequacy, and coherence. Reported comparisons between the graph-aware pipeline and the linear baseline use per-section paired comparisons and aggregated statistics; choice of specific statistical tests is given below (general background knowledge).

\smallskip
\textbf{Sampling and aggregation.}
For each experimental run we treat each generated section (node of the document graph) as the primary unit of analysis. When the experimental condition produces multiple variants for a given section we average automated metrics per variant and report both per-section and per-document aggregates. Where appropriate we stratify reporting by section type (e.g., methods, results, related work) to highlight differences in citation behavior across functional roles; stratification is descriptive and does not imply external generalizability beyond the evaluated domains.

\smallskip
\textbf{Annotation procedure for assertions and citations.}
Human annotators inspect each generated section and perform two complementary annotation passes:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Assertion segmentation: annotators mark spans corresponding to atomic factual assertions or claims within the section. An assertion is any sentence or clause that makes a verifiable factual statement used to support the section-level narrative.
  \item Citation linkage: for each marked assertion, annotators record whether the text contains an explicit inline source citation (e.g., a parenthetical or bracketed reference) or an explicit textual pointer to a retrieved source. If an inline citation is present, annotators additionally verify whether the cited source (from refs.bib or injected evidence) plausibly supports the assertion; this verification may require consulting the retrieved evidence snippets supplied during generation.
\end{enumerate}
An assertion is labeled as \emph{supported} if there exists an explicit inline citation that the annotator judges to plausibly support the claim; otherwise it is labeled \emph{unsupported}. All annotator judgments are recorded at the assertion level to enable fine-grained counting.

\smallskip
\textbf{Primary metrics.}
We compute the following primary metrics per section and then aggregate across the evaluation set.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Citation coverage (per section):} the fraction of assertions that are labeled supported.
    \[
      \mathrm{Coverage} = \frac{|\text{Supported Assertions}|}{|\text{Total Assertions}|}.
    \]
    This metric emphasizes explicit citation presence and annotator judgment of whether the cited source plausibly supports the assertion.

  \item \textbf{Hallucination rate (unsupported assertions per section):} the fraction (or count) of assertions labeled unsupported.
    \[
      \mathrm{HallucinationRate} = \frac{|\text{Unsupported Assertions}|}{|\text{Total Assertions}|}.
    \]
    We report both the per-section rate and the mean unsupported assertion count per section to capture prevalence and absolute burden for post-hoc audit.

  \item \textbf{Citation–assertion alignment score (automated audit):} an automated check that verifies whether every inline citation token in the generated LaTeX maps to an entry in the assembled refs.bib and whether the cited entries appear among the evidence snippets retrieved during generation. The check yields a precision-style ratio:
    \[
      \mathrm{CitationAlignment} = \frac{|\text{Citations mapped to evidence or refs.bib}|}{|\text{Inline citations in text}|}.
    \]
    Failures flag missing references or citations that point to no retrieved evidence.
\end{itemize}

\smallskip
\textbf{Reviewer-style quality rubric.}
Independent human reviewers rate each section on a small set of coarse-grained dimensions using ordinal scales (e.g., 1--5):
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Factuality:} degree to which the content appears factually correct and not contradicted by provided evidence.
  \item \emph{Citation adequacy:} degree to which claims are accompanied by appropriate citations and whether citations appear to substantiate claims.
  \item \emph{Coherence and clarity:} local coherence of the section and clarity of exposition.
  \item \emph{Overall quality:} holistic assessment of whether the section would require minor, moderate, or major edits to be acceptable in a draft manuscript.
\end{enumerate}
Per-section ordinal scores are averaged to produce mean reviewer scores per condition; we also report the proportion of sections rated below an acceptability threshold. The rubric and the mapping from ordinal scores to acceptability categories are fixed prior to annotation to avoid hindsight bias.

\smallskip
\textbf{Inter-annotator agreement and adjudication.}
A subset of sections is double-annotated to estimate inter-annotator agreement on assertion segmentation, supported/unsupported labels, and reviewer ratings. Agreement for binary labels (supported vs.\ unsupported) is summarized with Cohen's kappa; agreement for ordinal reviewer ratings is summarized with an appropriate ordinal agreement coefficient (general background knowledge). Disagreements on assertion support are resolved by a predefined adjudication step involving a senior annotator; adjudicated labels are used for primary reporting.

\smallskip
\textbf{Automated audits and tooling.}
Automated checks complement manual annotation by (i) verifying syntactic conformance to the JSON schema emitted by the generation pipeline, (ii) validating that every citation token references an entry in refs.bib, and (iii) performing exact- and fuzzy-string matching between asserted claims' key phrases and the titles/abstracts of cited evidence snippets to surface likely mismatches. Automated audits produce flags used to prioritize manual review but are not treated as ground truth for supported/unsupported labels without human confirmation.

\smallskip
\textbf{Statistical comparisons and uncertainty quantification.}
For paired per-section comparisons (same section produced by graph-aware and baseline pipelines) we use non-parametric paired tests and bootstrap confidence intervals to assess the robustness of observed differences (general background knowledge). Wherever possible we report effect sizes together with two-sided p-values and bootstrap-derived confidence intervals for medians or mean differences. All statistical choices, multiple-comparison corrections, and exact sample sizes are reported alongside results to support reproducibility.

\smallskip
\textbf{Reporting conventions and limitations of the protocol.}
All reported metrics are computed on the annotated evaluation set described in Section 4.1. We emphasize that citation coverage captures the presence of an explicit citation judged by annotators to plausibly support an assertion; it does not guarantee that the cited source fully substantiates the claim. Likewise, the hallucination rate reflects annotator judgments of unsupported assertions given available evidence and annotator access; retrieval failures can inflate measured hallucination. These caveats are discussed further in Section 6.2.
